Separation of Concerns

Structuring our solution by organizing it well. Let’s think about a data science workflow:

  • Data Acquisition - Keep data acquisition code separate from analysis and modeling code. Write the code to obtain the data and save the code and data for further use.
  • Data Cleaning and Preprocessing - In a different script or notebook, address missing values, encoding categorical variables, normalize numeric variables.
  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) - in a yet another notebook or script, explore the data and keep this separated from the data acquisition, cleaning, preprocessing etc.
  • Feature Engineering - We might write functions in yet another script to create new features and keep them separate from data acquisition, cleaning, preprocessing, EDA, modeling.
  • Model Training & Testing - yet another script or notebook where the actual modeling occurs.

How Separation of Concerns can help

  • Improves reproducibility (given the clarity of the solution).
  • Helps collaboration because team members can work on the parts independently.
  • Problems or improvements in one part should not affect the other parts
  • Scales up well because it will be easier to extend models, preprocessors, etc.

Writing Functions

Functions

  • Writing functions helps you with:
  • 1
  • 2
  • 3
  • 4
  • 5
  • 6
  • Reusing code and its logic without copying and pasting
    • Without functions or scripts you might be copying and pasting a lot.
    • Writing functions allows you to encapsulate your logic, making your programming reusable and easier to maintain.
    • Define your logic once and call on it many times
  • Efficiency and Automation
    • Python is excellent for automating repetitive tasks.
    • If you plan to work with data in the future or generate reports, presentations, etc. scripts can save time.
    • Example: Use Python to automate downloading data, cleaning the data, and then saving a formatted data analysis report.
  • Debugging and Error Handling
    • Using functions makes identifying errors easier because typically a function should only do one task well (separation of concern?) - this helps us isolate issues/problems.
    • Programming our own functions and writing scripts lets us log errors and identify errors – helps us to track down errors in our code
  • Scalability and Collaboration
    • Scripts and modularized code scale better for larger projects.
    • When working in a team, properly structured Python code is far easier to share and easier for others to understand.
  • Gaining access to advanced features of Python
    • Many Python libraries (e.g., pandas, NumPy) assume you are able to define functions, use classes, and write scripts.
    • Some machine learning models often require defining custom data transformations via object-oriented programming
  • Employability
    • Given the team-based work environment, many employers expect Python programmers to write structured, modular code
    • This means knowing how to write functions, using scripts, and implementing object-oriented programming (next week)
    • Programming languages come and go, but developing the underlying creative skills will serve you well.

def

This is the keyword for defining functions in Python

  • It must be followed by the function name and then a parenthesized list of formal parameters and a colon.
  • The statements that form the body of the function start at the next line, and must be indented.

def fib(n):    # write Fibonacci series less than n
    """Print a Fibonacci series less than n."""
    a, b = 0, 1 # unpacking a tuple
    while a < n:
        print(a, end=' ')
        a, b = b, a+b
    print()

Task Analysis on a Pet Age Calculator

  • Suppose a pet retailer has asked your team to program a Pet Age Calculator. They want a Python script that allows a user to input a pet’s age in years after selecting pet type (dog, cat, hamster, bird), and then converts the pet’s age to an estimated human equivalent. They have supplied the formulas:
    • 15 human years equals the first year of a medium-sized dog’s life. Year two for a dog equals about nine years for a human. And after that, each human year would be approximately five years for a dog
    • A cat’s first year is 15 human years, the second year adds 9 more, and each year after that is roughly equivalent to 4 human years
    • For a hamster, every 14 days of life is equivalent to a human year
    • Multiply bird age by 5 to estimate the human equivalent.
  • Please suggest ways to break this down into a set of subproblems.
    • How should you structure the calculations? One big function for all four animals or one for each type?
    • Will you need other libraries to calculate age?
    • How should you capture the animal’s type and age? I haven’t taught this to you, but would your team want a GUI for users to input information? (…ask a chatbot?)

"""
should have a docstring about here
"""

def dog_to_human_years(dog_age):
    """15 human years equals the first year of a 
    medium-sized dog’s life.
    Year two for a dog equals about nine years for a human.
    And after that, each human year would be 
    approximately five years for a dog."""
    pass

def bird_to_human_years(bird_age):
    if bird_age <= 0:
        return "Age must be a positive number."
    return f"Your bird is {bird_age * 5} in human years"

def pet_age_calculator():   
    """Calculates the human age of the pet based on the pet type and ask the user for input"""
    print("Welcome to the Pet Age Calculator!")
    print("Supported pets are: Dog, Bird")

    pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ").strip().lower()

    if pet_type in ["dog", "bird"]:
            pet_age = int(input(f"Enter your {pet_type}'s age in years: "))
        
            if pet_type == "dog":
                human_age = dog_to_human_years(pet_age)
            elif pet_type == "bird":
                human_age = bird_to_human_years(pet_age)

            print(f"Your {pet_type} is approximately {human_age} human years old!")
    else:
        print("Sorry, this calculator only supports dogs and birds.")

# run it
if __name__ == "__main__":
    pet_age_calculator()

More on writing Functions

Local, Enclosing, & Global Scope

  • Before we move to errors, it is useful to discuss LEGB
  • Stands for Local, Enclosing, Global and Built-In
  • And refers to the order in which Python resolves variable names.
  • Understanding this order will help with the debugging of errors when writing our functions.
  • And decrease frustration/build confidence

A symbol table

The built-in function locals() can reveal the symbol table.

Code 
def my_function():
    x = 10  
    y = 20
    print(locals())  # Print the local symbol table

my_function()
print(x) # throws a NameError
{'x': 10, 'y': 20}
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[9], line 7
      4     print(locals())  # Print the local symbol table
      6 my_function()
----> 7 print(x) # throws a NameError

NameError: name 'x' is not defined
  • Here, x and y exist only inside the function named my_function().

What a symbol table is/does

  • A symbol table is a Python data structure
  • Python uses it to store information on variables, functions, classes
  • Python absolutely needs it to operate
  • There are different levels of symbol table

Local/Enclosing/Global

This is the hierarchy:

  1. Local (L) – First, Python looks inside the function’s symbol table for variables.
  2. Enclosing (E) – If it’s a nested function, Python looks in the surrounding function’s symbol table.
  3. Global (G) – Then it checks the global (top level) scope.
  4. Built-in (B) – Finally, Python checks Python’s built-in functions.

Example LEGB at work

Code 
a = "global"

def outer():
    b = "enclosing"
    
    def inner():
        c = "local"
        print("--- INNER FUNCTION SCOPE DIAGNOSTICS ---")
        print(f"{'Name':<12} {'Found?':<8} {'Where?'}")
        print("-" * 35)
        for name in ['c', 'b', 'a', 'print', 'inner', 'outer']:
            if name in locals():
                where = "Local"
            elif 'b' in outer.__code__.co_varnames and name == 'b':
                where = "Enclosing"
            elif name in globals():
                where = "Global"
            elif name in dir(__builtins__):
                where = "Built-in"
            else:
                where = "Not Found"
            found = where != "Not Found"
            print(f"{name:<12} {str(found):<8} {where}")

    inner()
    # outer() # will throw a recursion error
    print(f" \n")
    print("--- ENCLOSING FUNCTION SCOPE DIAGNOSTICS ---")
    print(f"{'Name':<12} {'Found?':<8} {'Where?'}")
    print("-" * 35)
    for name in ['c', 'b', 'a', 'print','inner', 'outer']:
        if name in locals():
            where = "Local"
        elif name in globals():
            where = "Global"
        elif name in dir(__builtins__):
            where = "Built-in"
        else:
            where = "Not Found"
        found = where != "Not Found"
        print(f"{name:<12} {str(found):<8} {where}")

# inner() # placed here throws a NameError
outer() # no recursion error here
print(f" \n")
print("--- OUTER FUNCTION SCOPE DIAGNOSTICS ---")
print(f"{'Name':<12} {'Found?':<8} {'Where?'}")
print("-" * 35)
for name in ['c', 'b', 'a', 'print','inner','outer']:
    if name in locals():
        where = "Local"
    elif name in globals():
        where = "Global"
    elif name in dir(__builtins__):
        where = "Built-in"
    else:
        where = "Not Found"
    found = where != "Not Found"
    print(f"{name:<12} {str(found):<8} {where}")
--- INNER FUNCTION SCOPE DIAGNOSTICS ---
Name         Found?   Where?
-----------------------------------
c            True     Local
b            True     Enclosing
a            True     Global
print        True     Built-in
inner        False    Not Found
outer        True     Global
 

--- ENCLOSING FUNCTION SCOPE DIAGNOSTICS ---
Name         Found?   Where?
-----------------------------------
c            False    Not Found
b            True     Local
a            True     Global

b            False    Not Found
a            True     Local
print        True     Built-in
inner        False    Not Found

Takeaways LEGB

  • Global variables and variables of enclosing functions can be referenced or passed inside of a function.
  • Global variables and variables of enclosing functions cannot be directly assigned a value or modified within a function
  • Unless… for the global variables they are named in a global statement, or, for variables of enclosing functions, named in a nonlocal statement.
  • You should know/understand the LEGB hierarchy but using the global or nonlocal statements can make Python code harder to read, debug, maintain and may have unexpected consequences.

Common Errors

  • SyntaxError – incorrect syntax.
  • IndentationError – when indentation is incorrect.
  • NameError - undefined or misspelled variable.
  • UnboundLocalError - modifying a variable before defining it.
  • TypeError - operation performed on an object of the wrong type.
  • ValueError – a function receives an argument of the correct type but an inappropriate value.
  • IndexError – accessing an invalid index in a sequence.
  • AttributeError – when an object does not have the requested attribute.
  • ImportError – when a module cannot be imported (might need to be installed)
  • ZeroDivisionError – dividing by zero.

Try/Except

  • You are just starting to write Python functions
  • The try/except system is like a safety net
    • You “try” risky code/uncertain
    • You plan to catch specific errors with “except”
    • You tell Python what it will print in response
    • Helps prevent your program from completely crashing.

Simple Example - Volume again

Code 
"""
computing sphere volume
"""

import math

PI = math.pi

r_input = input("What is the radius of your sphere? ")

try:
    r = float(r_input)
    if r > 0:
        volume = round((4/3) * PI * (r**3), 2)
        print(f"The volume of your sphere is {volume} cubic units.")
    else:
        print("Error: The radius must be a positive numerical value.")
except ValueError:
    print("Error: Please enter a valid numerical value for the radius.")

If a user is entering bad values like 0 or a string, a specific message is returned.

import requests

def fetch_weather():
     try:

        print("Failed to connect to the weather server.")

Fixing the pet calculator

  • As a Python programmer you may decide to throw (raise) an exception when a condition occurs. To do this, use the raise keyword.
Code 
def dog_to_human_years(dog_age):
    """15 human years equals the first year of a 
    medium-sized dog’s life.
    Year two for a dog equals about nine years for a human.
    And after that, each human year would be 
    approximately five years for a dog."""
    if dog_age <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Age must be a positive number.")
        # return "Age must be a positive number." # Not this way
    elif dog_age == 1:
        return 15
    elif dog_age == 2:
        return 24
    else:
        return 24 + (dog_age - 2) * 5

def bird_to_human_years(bird_age):
    if bird_age <= 0:
       raise ValueError("Age must be a positive number.")
       #return "Age must be a positive number." # Not this way
    return f"Your bird is {bird_age * 5} in human years"

def pet_age_calculator():   
    """Calculates the human age of the pet based on the pet type and ask the user for input"""
    print("Welcome to the Pet Age Calculator!")
    print("Supported pets are: Dog, Bird")

    pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ").strip().lower()

    if pet_type in ["dog", "bird"]:
        try:
            pet_age = int(input(f"Enter your {pet_type}'s age in years: "))
            if pet_type == "dog":
                human_age = dog_to_human_years(pet_age)
            elif pet_type == "bird":
                human_age = bird_to_human_years(pet_age)
            print(f"Your {pet_type} is approximately {human_age} human years old!")
        except ValueError as e:
            print(f"Error: {e}")
    else:
        print("Sorry, this calculator only supports dogs and birds.")

# run it
if __name__ == "__main__":
    pet_age_calculator()

Structure of the Previous examples

  • Designed to address multiple types of failures
  • Some were specific to internet related issues
  • Provides interpretable error handling
  • Will prevent a complete crash of our code
  • Uses except ValueError: Catches the error
  • Uses except ValueError as e: Catches the error AND give it a custom message so you can examine it further

Recommendations from Python.org

PEP 8 is the style guide. Clear code is easier to debug than unclear. Main points of PEP 8:

  • Use 4-space indentation, and no tabs.

  • Wrap lines so that they don’t exceed 79 characters.

  • Use blank lines to separate functions and classes, and larger blocks of code inside functions.

  • When possible, put comments on a line of their own.

  • Use docstrings.

  • Use spaces around operators and after commas, but not directly inside bracketing constructs: a = f(1, 2) + g(3, 4).

  • Name your classes and functions consistently; the convention is to use UpperCamelCase for classes and lowercase_with_underscores for functions and methods.

More data structures

Additional builtin data structures

  • Tuples - iterable sequences, immutable
  • Dictionaries - iterable, unordered collection, mutable
  • Sets - iterable, ordered collection, mutable

Tuples

A Tuple is an immutable sequence, this means:

  • It cannot be modified once created, you can make a new one
  • Its elements have a definite order.
  • A tuple can be indexed and sliced using index notation.
  • Like a list, it can have mixed types of data
  • Iterable

Tuples v Lists

A Tuple is a lot like a list, but:

  • Tuples are immutable, Lists are mutable
  • Tuples need slightly less memory
  • Tuples iterate a little faster
  • Tuples are useful for fixed data that should be unchanging (e.g., an ID number)
  • (optional) Tuple immutablility also allows the tuple to be hashable (hashable means to have a stable and unique integer representation throughout its existence) if all of its elements are hashable.

Tuple operations

  • Slice
  • Max/Min
  • Convert

phy_sci_tuple = tuple(phy_sci_list)
print(f"Is phy_sci_tuple a tuple? {isinstance(phy_sci_tuple, tuple)}")
Is phy_sci_list a list? True
Is phy_sci_tuple a tuple? True

Example Tuple applications

  • Constant
  • Keys
  • Swap
  • Return Multiple values

You can easily swap two values using a tuple

Code 
a, b = 5, 10
print(f"The original a, b is {a, b}")

a, b = b, a
print(f"The tuple swap is {a, b}")  # Output: 10, 5
The original a, b is (5, 10)
The tuple swap is (10, 5)

This is handy, in your functions, you can return multiple values using a tuple:

Code 
def divide(a, b):
    quotient = a // b
    remainder = a % b
    return quotient, remainder  # Returns a tuple

x, y = divide(10, 3)
print(f"quotient: {x}, remainder: {y}") 
quotient: 3, remainder: 1

Sets

  • Sets are iterable but not sequences
  • Sets are unordered and cannot be indexed
  • Sets cannot have duplicates
  • Sets are mutable
  • Sets are used where order and duplicate values don’t matter

Set applications

  • in
  • Intersection
  • Difference
  • uniqueness
  • Membership testing is very fast
Code 
import time

# Large list vs tuple
large_set = set(range(10**6))
large_list = list(range(10**6))
large_tuple = tuple(range(10**6))


# Measure list iteration time
start = time.time()
999999 in large_list
end = time.time()
print(f"List iteration took: {end - start:.6f} seconds")

# Measure tuple iteration time
start = time.time()
999999 in large_tuple
end = time.time()
print(f"Tuple iteration took: {end - start:.6f} seconds")

# Measure set iteration time
start = time.time()
999999 in large_set
end = time.time()
print(f"Set iteration took: {end - start:.6f} seconds")
List iteration took: 0.007270 seconds
Tuple iteration took: 0.006188 seconds
Set iteration took: 0.000024 seconds
  • Finding the intersection of two sets is fast
Code 
import time

large_set_A = set([range(10**6), -6])
large_set_B = set([range(10**6+1,10**6+10**6+1), -6])

start = time.time()
set_numbers = large_set_A & large_set_B  
end = time.time()
print(f"Set intersection took: {end - start:.6f} seconds")

print(set_numbers)  # Output: {-6}  
Set intersection took: 0.000019 seconds
{-6}
  • Finding the difference of two sets
  • Something that list and tuples cannot do (programmers convert lists and tuples to sets if possible)

Dictionary

  • A data structure with an unordered, mutable, and indexed collection of key-value pairs.
  • A each value (name, number, anything really) in the dictionary has a label (called a key) and a value.
  • The key-value pair allows us to store and retrieve values using unique keys (efficient for lookups by name not by position)
  • Create using {} or dict()
  • Keys must be immutable types (strings, numbers, tuples)
  • Values can be any data type (lists, strings, numbers, tuples, other dictionaries, etc.).

import re # regular expressions (later)

file_path = "gettysburg.txt" 

# Open and read the file creating a string

LEGB, indentation, scope, again

  • LEGB and Indentation are intertwined
    • Indentation defines the boundaries of functions and blocks.
    • Python determines scope (variable access) based on function definitions and indentation
    • Since each indentation level can create a new scope - if we declare a variable inside an indented block (like a function), it is only accessible within that block unless explicitly returned (or modified using global or nonlocal).

Another Function & Scope Example

  • mu1
  • mu2
  • mu3
  • mu4

  • Why can’t I get mu?
Code 
# Example
data = list(range(2, 50, 2)) # Example dataset
x = 20  # Data point for which we want the Z-score

def mean(data):
    return sum(data) / len(data)

def standard_deviation(data):
    mu = mean(data)
    variance = sum((x - mu) ** 2 for x in data) / len(data)  # Population formula
    return variance ** 0.5

def z_score(x, data):
    mu = mean(data)
    sigma = standard_deviation(data)
    return (x - mu) / sigma

print(f"mean of the data is: {mean(data):.4f}")
print(f"SD of the data is: {standard_deviation(data):.4f}")
print(f"Z-score of {x}: {z_score(x, data):.4f}")
print(f"x is {x}")

print(f"but why won't mu {mu} print?") # NameError

NameError: name 'mu' is not defined

standard deviation is trying to find “mu” in its local scope (not there), failing that, it moves to its enclosing score (in this example, global) and it cannot find it there as well so a NameError is the result.

Code 
# Example
data = list(range(2, 50, 2)) # Example dataset
x = 20  # single Data point for the Z-score

def mean(data):
    mu = sum(data) / len(data)
    return mu

def standard_deviation(data, mu):
    variance = sum((x - mu) ** 2 for x in data) / len(data)  # Population standard deviation
    return variance ** 0.5

def z_score(x, data, mu):
    sigma = standard_deviation(data, mu)
    return (x - mu) / sigma

# this works, the other functions can see mu
print(f"mean of the data is: {mean(data):.4f}")
print(f"SD of the data is: {standard_deviation(data, mean(data)):.4f}")
print(f"Z-score of {x}: {z_score(x, data, mean(data)):.4f}")
print(f"x is {x}")

print(f"but why won't mu {mu} print?")

NameError: name 'mu' is not defined

This works because mu is properly passed to the other two functions but it will not print because it’s not in the global scope.

  • make global (call it mu2) OR (absolute last resort) use global keyword
Code 
# constants
data = list(range(2, 50, 2)) # Example dataset
x = 20  # Data point for which we want the Z-score

def mean(data):
    global mu
    mu = sum(data) / len(data)
    return mu

mu2 = mean(data)

def standard_deviation(data):
    variance = sum((x - mu2) ** 2 for x in data) / len(data)  # Population standard deviation
    return variance ** 0.5

def z_score(x, data):
    sigma = standard_deviation(data)
    return (x - mu2) / sigma


print(f"mean of the data is: {mean(data):.4f}")
print(f"SD of the data is: {standard_deviation(data):.4f}")
print(f"Z-score of {x}: {z_score(x, data):.4f}")
print(f"x is {x}")
print(f"but mu2 {mu2} prints")
print(f"and mu {mu} prints having been made global")
mean of the data is: 25.0000
SD of the data is: 13.8444
Z-score of 20: -0.3612
x is 20
but mu2 25.0 prints
and mu 25.0 prints having been made global
  • To avoid frustration & errors one must understand where Python expects to find and store variables when used inside a function.
  • If you assign a value to a variable inside a function, Python assumes it is a local variable.
  • If Python assumes a variable is local, but the variable actually originates from an enclosing or global scope, you get an UnboundLocalError.
  • If the variable doesn’t exist at all or not visible at all, a NameError will result

A benefit of arguments

  • When you pass a variable as an argument to a function, Python doesn’t care whether it’s global, enclosing, or local
  • To Python, function arguments are just values being copied into the function’s local symbol table.
  • So if scoping rules confuse you, a possible solution is to program functions with arguments

But beware of mutable objects (lists, dictionaries)

  • Python does not pass arguments by “value” or “reference”, but instead passes “references to objects.” This means:
    • If the object is immutable (like int, str, tuple), Python creates a new local copy.
    • If the object is mutable (like list, dict), modifications inside the function affect the original object.

Examples using mutable list

You can use lists, just be aware of their behavior.

  • Nested list
  • Nested List reassigned
  • shallow copied
  • shallow fail
  • deepcopy
Code 
original_list = [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]]  # Global list

def modify_list(lst):
    lst.append(6)  # Modifies the original list.
    return lst

new_list = modify_list(original_list)

print(new_list)
print(original_list)  # prints [1, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6] globally
[1, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6]
[1, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6]
Code 
original_list = [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]] # Global list

def modify_list(lst):
    new_list = original_list
    new_list.append(6)  
    new_list[0] = 10
    return new_list

new_list = modify_list(original_list)

print(new_list) # modified
print(original_list)  # modified too
[10, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6]
[10, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6]
Code 
original_list = [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]] # Global list

def modify_list(lst):
    new_list = original_list.copy()
    new_list.append(6)  
    new_list[0] = 10
    return new_list

new_list = modify_list(original_list)

print(new_list) # modified
print(original_list)  # prints [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]]
[10, 2, 3, [4, 5], 6]
[1, 2, 3, [4, 5]]

Unfortunately, if you modify the nested elements…

Code 
original_list = [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]] # Global list

def modify_list(lst):
    new_list = original_list.copy()
    new_list.append(6)  
    new_list[0] = 10
    new_list[3][0] = 40 # this happens
    return new_list

new_list = modify_list(original_list)

print(new_list) # modified
print(original_list)  # prints [1, 2, 3, [40, 5]]
[10, 2, 3, [40, 5], 6]
[1, 2, 3, [40, 5]]

Use the copy module from the Python Standard Library and it’s deepcopy function:

Code 
import copy

original_list = [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]] # Global list

def modify_list(lst):
    new_list = copy.deepcopy(original_list)
    new_list.append(6)  
    new_list[0] = 10
    new_list[3][0] = 40 
    return new_list

new_list = modify_list(original_list)

print(new_list) # modified
print(original_list)  # stays unmodified
[10, 2, 3, [40, 5], 6]
[1, 2, 3, [4, 5]]

Back to Parameters & Arguments

One of the most important and useful functions in Python has very many parameters (you don’t need this many):

Some definitions

  • Parameter: A variable that is in a function definition. It acts as a stand-n for the value that will be passed when the function is called.

  • Argument: When the function is called the argument is the actual value passed to it.

As you can see from the read_csv() example, one can program a function to have multiple parameters which can accept multiple arguments.

Example: Multiple arguments

You’ve seen this about two lectures ago. What if we rewrite it to have multiple parameters? Orginally, name was only parameter. We could add the number of attempts and even a text to print out.

Code 
def name_to_a1z26(name = None, attempts=3, suggestion="Too many invalid attempts. Please try again later"):
    while attempts > 0:
        if not name or name.strip() == "":
            name = input("Enter your name (or type 'exit' to quit): ")
        
        if name.lower() == "exit":
            print("Exiting the script")
            return

        elif name.isalpha():  # Check the name is in A-Z or a-z after removing spaces
            cipher_values = [ord(char) - 64 for char in name if char.isalpha()]
            print(f"Your name in A1Z26 cipher is: {cipher_values}")
            return

        attempts -= 1
        print(f"Invalid input. {attempts} attempts left.")

        if attempts == 0:
            print(suggestion)
            return
        
        name = None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    name_to_a1z26()

(aside) if name == “main”:

  • Recall - inclusion of if __name__ == "__main__": stops accidental execution if this script is imported into another program.
  • Is useful when testing. Here it is imported into the REPL:
